description: Rize, an initiative dedicated to democratizing access to STEM. This NASA Space Apps project will serve as a prototype within the Rize ecosystem, directly tackling the challenge: "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer."
summary:
Spacock Invaders is a retrofuturistic web game inspired by classic space shooters from the 2000s, Chicken Invaders. It is designed to initiate junior astronauts in data-based decision-making, teamwork, and leadership in STEM areas.

The player chooses a route (Earth orbit, space station, or moon) and a position: Gigi pilots and dodges asteroids; Ceece interprets the radar and warns of safe routes; Uki, the AI of the ship, distributes solar energy between shields, life support, communications, and science, and sends oxygen. If Gigi or Ceece lose energy or contact, Uki takes command: he pilots or forwards the alerts.

Turn real limitations into gameplay: no choice is free. More shield means less science; sending oxygen empties the tank. Solar gusts come from NASA DONKI and Asteroids from NASA NeoWs. Gusts cut the radio, Earth's warnings arrive with the actual light delay, and radiation is measured in milisieverts.

It matters because space education usually remains in abstract data. Here the children live the dilemmas of a mission planner, and the final report shows the cost of each decision.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Spacock Invaders is a browser-based space mission simulator for kids aged 7 to 12. It starts by switching on a retro monitor. Then the player picks a route: Earth orbit (3 min), the Space Station (5 min) or the Moon (7 min). The farther you go, the more science you can do, but also the more radiation and the longer the communication delay.

Next, the player picks a station on the ship. The AI runs the other two:

  • Gigi (Combat): flies the ship and dodges asteroids and solar flares. Shooting uses energy.
  • Ceece (Detection): reads the radar and a sensor table with NASA data, and tells Gigi which lane is safe.
  • Uki (Resources): the ship's AI. She splits 10 units of solar power between life support, shields, comms and science, and sends oxygen and energy to the crew.

When an asteroid hits the ship, a roulette picks which section loses its screen for 30 seconds. If it lands on Gigi, she has 6 seconds to hand control to Uki. Solar flares can knock out the radio, and if Ceece loses contact, Uki relays the alerts. At the end, a mission report explains what each decision cost, comparing the radiation received to chest X-rays and to days on the Space Station.

Real NASA data

  • NASA DONKI: every solar storm in the game is a real solar flare. Its class (C, M, or X) sets how much radiation it carries and whether it knocks out the radio.
  • NASA NeoWs: asteroids carry the names, sizes and speeds of real asteroids passing near Earth.
  • Offline: without internet, the game uses an archive of real events and says so on screen ("ARCHIVE" instead of "LIVE").

Benefits

  • Makes the hard trade-offs of a real mission tangible: no choice is free.
  • Builds data-driven decision-making, teamwork and leadership when something fails.
  • Explains science terms (millisieverts, magnetosphere, flare classes, light delay) in plain language, inside the game.
  • Needs no downloads or accounts, so it's easy to use in classrooms and at home.

Expected impact

We want kids to finish a game understanding a real limit of survival in space, not just having played a fun game. It's built for schools, STEM workshops and families. Because real solar activity changes, every mission is different and worth replaying with a new strategy. Next, we plan a multiplayer mode.

Tools used

  • Game:
    • HTML5, CSS3 and vanilla JavaScript, with Canvas 2D for graphics and the Web Audio API for sound.
    • NASA APIs (DONKI and NeoWs) via api.nasa.gov.
    • Google Fonts (Orbitron, VT323, Share Tech Mono).
    • Visual Studio Code and GitHub, hosted on Cloudflare.
    • Automated Playwright playtests to balance the difficulty.
    • AI assistance (Claude & Qwen) for coding.
  • Demo video: Python, Playwright, FFmpeg, Piper TTS voice and music synthesized with NumPy and SciPy.
  • Art: the team's original illustrations of Ceece, Gigi and Uki. Procreate (iPad Pro)
  • Hardware: a personal computer (Mac mini).

How is it creative?

  • It blends a classic arcade shooter with a retro-futuristic mission-control dashboard, inside a monitor that boots up like an old computer.
  • Each role experiences the same problem from a different angle: flying, reading data or managing resources.
  • The impact roulette and the handover of command to Uki turn failures into leadership moments.
  • The real data isn't decoration: it changes the game.

What did our team consider?

  • Age: only 3 core resources (oxygen, energy, shields) so kids aged 7 to 12 aren't overwhelmed.
  • No "safe" option: every decision has a cost, as in real mission planning.
  • Honesty about data: the game shows when data is live and when it comes from the archive. Anything fictional, like the black hole, is labeled in the manual.
  • Learning from failure: losing isn't punishing; the final report teaches what happened.
  • Accessibility: it works with keyboard, mouse or touch, has a pause button with a manual, and adapts to computers and phones.
